newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. students to put Chinese high schools on line.
newsitem.headline: U.S. students to put Chinese high schools on line.

text.p: Students from a leading U.S. university have received permission to link up Chinese secondary schools to the Internet and teach students how to run their own websites, the students said on Friday.

The 13 technology evangelists are students from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Boston who will come to China during their summer break in July and August to hook up five of China's top high schools.

"At MIT, we're blessed with this opportunity to learn a lot about technology, and we felt we had something we could share with other students," said MIT computer science student Ron Cao, contacted by telephone in Boston.
The students will put on line two high schools in Shanghai, two in Beijing, and one in the western China city of Xi'an.

It follows a 1996 project in which Cao and another student spent six weeks in Shanghai helping students at the Number Two High School to set up their own Internet server, making it the first Chinese high school to be linked to the Internet, he said.
The website address of the Shanghai high school is http://202.120.80.2.

"The focus will be on getting equipment up and running and teaching the students how to operate the equipment, connecting them to the Internet, and teaching Java and other high level languages," said Roger Hu, another of the students involved in the project.
"Another project is setting up a Java chat page so that students from different high schools can meet on the same page and talk to each other," Hu said.
Access to the global computer network is still limited in China.

There are estimated to be up to 100,000 Internet access accounts in China, and the Chinese systems ban access to many parts of the Internet, including all news groups and other sites that are considered politically or socially unacceptable.
But Cao said they had found last year that there was a lot of support for development of the Internet access in China from both ordinary people and officials.

"Teachers were all very excited about getting on the Internet," he said. "What they were concerned about was lack of money and people to understand technology. In fact people in China seem very pro-Internet."
The MIT students said they expected the Internet to eventually become as central to the lives of Chinese students as it is for them.
"In China, people talk about the dangers of exposing people to the Internet, but we're looking at it from an educational point of view," said Roger Hu.
"There's so much out there on the Internet to learn, so many websites, that it should make a huge difference in terms of education if students were allowed to tap into that resource," he said.
